transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Could you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah, hi. Um... I guess I'm here because of... well, my face. 

There's this rough, sunken-looking patch on it. I just... I can't stop seeing it whenever I look in the mirror, or if there's a photo. It makes one side of me look real old and beat-up. People keep telling me they barely notice anything, but... yeah. That's why I'm here, I guess.
Do you find yourself doing anything repeatedly, like checking mirrors, trying to cover it up, or comparing your face to others, because of your concern about that patch on your face?

Yeah... I guess. Um... like before work, or if I'm supposed to go over to my sister's for game night. I just... I end up checking the bathroom mirror a lot. Kind of turning my head to see how the light catches it. Rubbing at the spot, trying to... I don't know. 

If I think it's looking too obvious, I'll just pull my hat down low. Or... sometimes I just make an excuse and don't go at all.
How much time would you say you spend each day thinking about that patch on your face, and does it really bother you or affect things you do?

Um... time? I don't know exactly. A lot, I guess. It's... it's always kind of there in the back of my head. 

As for affecting things... yeah. I mean, I've been late heading out to the site a few times because I'm stuck looking at it. And... well, I try to stay out of the way if the guys are taking pictures at work. Like I said before, I've skipped out on game night with my sister a few times, too. I just... I don't really want people staring at my face. It bothers me.

latest_inference.note: The patient's preoccupation with a perceived defect in appearance, along with repetitive behaviors such as mirror checking and avoidance of social situations, strongly supports a diagnosis of Body Dysmorphic Disorder (F45.22). Other candidates (L98.9, F40.00, F32.9) are ruled out due to insufficient evidence or better explanation from the current history.
